## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

*Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Sekhiya 74* (*Hariteuccāra*) is the seventy-fourth training rule in the *Sekhiya* section of the Pali Vinaya Piṭaka's Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga. The rule enjoins a monastic not to defecate, urinate, or spit upon cultivated plants or green crops (*harita*) unless they are ill [Hüsken 1997]. In the Vinaya's word commentary, *harita* is defined as planted grain and vegetables that constitute food for people [Hüsken 1997]. Non-compliance constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense for both monks and nuns [Hüsken 1997]. The non-offense (*anāpatti*) clauses provide exemptions if the monastic is sick, or if the waste is deposited on ground with little or sparse vegetation (*appaharita*) and subsequently covered up [Hüsken 1997].

Modern scholars have discussed the rule in the context of early Buddhist monastic ethics and environmental attitudes. Damien Keown references Sekhiya 74 alongside rules such as Pācittiya 11 as Vinaya prohibitions against damaging plant life and vegetation [Keown 1992]. Shravasti Dhammika links Sekhiya 74 and Sekhiya 75 to broader ascetic contexts and pre-Buddhist attitudes regarding the sentience or protection of plants and living entities [Dhammika]. Modern English translations include that of Bhikkhu Brahmali.

 In DharmaNexus's text-reuse analysis, the rule shares 145 matching passages with 42 other Pali texts, exhibiting its closest formulaic overlaps with adjacent rules regarding bodily waste and hygiene such as Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Sekhiya 75, Sekhiya 73, and Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Sekhiya 75 [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, DharmaNexus identifies textual alignment with Jayarakṣita's Sanskrit commentary *Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā* [DharmaNexus].
